newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S GAME PARK BLAZE GOOD FOR NATURE - RANGERS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S GAME PARK BLAZE GOOD FOR NATURE - RANGERS.

text.p: A wild bush fire that engulfed vast areas of South Africa's Kruger National Park game reserve was an entirely natural phenomenon and would benefit the park, rangers said on Thursday.
"This was a completely natural fire and it was not a bad thing to have happened because the park needs fires," Chief Ranger Bruce Bryden told Reuters.

He said estimates that a quarter of the premier tourist attraction had been burnt by Wednesday were overdone. Some 15 percent of the 20,000 sq km (7,700 sq mile) park, home to thousands of animals and birds, had been affected.
"It is not a raging fire any more and we expect it to burn out in the next couple of days," Bryden said.
Lightning a week ago sparked four fires which were fanned by strong winds and high temperatures in the southern half of the 60-year-old reserve.
It is the worst fire for 40 years.
The fire had moved at moderate speed, hopefully giving most big game, numerous impala and smaller animals and insects time to flee, the ranger said.

Without natural fires, grass would grow too long and begin to rot, denying grazing animals food. Some areas would grow dense shrubs which would also affect animal feeding and movement patterns, Bryden said.
"It would be bad for the park if there were no fires," he said.

The fire burned erratically as winds changed direction several times and day-time temperatures dropped, leaving islands of untouched vegetation in burnt-out areas, Bryden said, adding: "Its not as terrible as it seems."
With vast areas of the park cleared of bush by the fire visitors would be able to see animals more easily, he said.

Kruger's statistics are impressive: 147 different species of mammals and 510 bird species, ranging from turkey-like ground hornbills to orange-eyed, shimmering starlings as well as 120,000 impala, 7,500 elephant, 900 leopards and more than 200 cheetah.
The park, which attracts some 700,000 visitors annually, also has 336 species of indigenous trees, 112 species of shrubs, more than 1,000 herb species and a profusion of flowers after seasonal rains.
